title: Getting started with ansible-dev-tools
shortDescription: Understand the ansible-dev-tools toolchain, compare its upstream and Red Hat delivery paths, and install the Red Hat-provided package on RHEL 9.
description: Learn how ansible-dev-tools assembles a coordinated Ansible content-development toolchain, how upstream and Red Hat delivery paths differ, and how to install and validate the Red Hat-provided package on RHEL 9.
audience: For Ansible content developers, platform engineers preparing supported development workstations, administrators evaluating upstream and Red Hat delivery paths, and learners who are comfortable with basic Linux package management.
coverAlt: Ansible development workflow showing connected create, lint, test, build, run, and sign stages
seoTitle: Install Red Hat ansible-dev-tools on RHEL 9
seoDescription: Understand ansible-dev-tools, compare its upstream and Red Hat delivery paths, then install and validate the Red Hat RPM on RHEL 9.
outcomes: Explain the purpose of the ansible-dev-tools package
Identify the role of each user-facing tool in the suite
Explain what the coordinated installation reduces and what it does not guarantee
Choose between the upstream and Red Hat delivery paths
Install and functionally validate the Red Hat-provided toolchain on RHEL 9

overview.title: What is ansible-dev-tools?
overview.introduction: ansible-dev-tools, commonly shortened to ADT, is a curated toolkit for developers who create and test Ansible content. It brings together independently released tools for scaffolding projects, linting and testing content, building and running execution environments, and signing automation. An execution environment is a container image that packages ansible-core, collections, Python dependencies, and system dependencies so automation can run consistently. ADT includes tools for building and using execution environments, but installing ADT does not create or validate one automatically. The tools remain separate projects, while ADT provides a coordinated way to install them and inspect the versions available in a development environment.
overview.itemsLabel: User-facing tools in the curated suite

items.title: ansible-core
items.detail: The minimal automation engine and command-line runtime. It parses inventories and playbooks, loads plugins and modules, and executes automation from a control node.

items.title: ansible-builder
items.detail: Builds containerized execution environments from a definition file. It resolves Ansible collections plus Python and operating-system dependencies into a repeatable image.

items.title: ansible-creator
items.detail: Scaffolds playbook projects, collections, roles, plugins, and related files. It gives new content a consistent structure instead of making authors assemble it by hand.

items.title: ansible-dev-environment
items.detail: Creates and manages isolated workspaces for Ansible content development. Its ade command installs collections and Python dependencies so Ansible and test tools can discover them together.

items.title: ansible-lint
items.detail: Checks playbooks, roles, and collections for syntax problems, risky patterns, and practices that reduce maintainability. Some findings can be corrected automatically.

items.title: ansible-navigator
items.detail: Provides a terminal interface for running and inspecting Ansible content, especially with execution environments. It can show play results, inventories, configuration, documentation, and images.

items.title: ansible-sign
items.detail: Signs and verifies Ansible project content. It helps establish whether protected files still match a trusted signing record before the content is used.

items.title: Molecule
items.detail: Runs scenario-based functional tests for roles, playbooks, and collections. A scenario can create test instances, apply automation, verify the result, and clean up.

items.title: pytest-ansible
items.detail: Extends pytest for Ansible development. It supports collection unit tests, Ansible-aware fixtures, and Python tests for modules and plugins.

items.title: tox-ansible
items.detail: Builds tox test matrices across Python and ansible-core versions. Collection authors use it to run sanity, unit, and integration tests in isolated combinations.

proof.title: Follow the Ansible content-development journey
proof.introduction: The tools in ADT support different stages of content development. This HOD proves the create and lint stages; the remaining stages require their own project-specific validation before the toolchain is accepted for wider use.

items.title: Create
items.detail: ansible-creator scaffolds playbook projects, collections, roles, plugins, and related development files.

items.title: Lint
items.detail: ansible-lint checks content for syntax problems, risky patterns, and maintainability issues.

items.title: Test
items.detail: Molecule, pytest-ansible, and tox-ansible exercise content across scenarios, fixtures, and version matrices.

items.title: Build
items.detail: ansible-builder assembles execution-environment images from declared collection, Python, and operating-system dependencies.

items.title: Run and inspect
items.detail: ansible-core executes automation, while ansible-navigator runs and inspects content with or without an execution environment.

items.title: Sign
items.detail: ansible-sign signs and verifies protected project content against an established trust process.

prerequisites.label: System
prerequisites.detail: A current, fully updated RHEL 9 physical or virtual machine using the x86_64 or AArch64 architecture. Enable the Ansible Automation Platform repository that matches the host architecture.

prerequisites.label: Access
prerequisites.detail: A non-root user that can run administrative commands with sudo to register the host, manage repositories, and install RPM packages.

prerequisites.label: Subscription access
prerequisites.detail: A Red Hat account with access to RHEL content and an Ansible Automation Platform subscription or product trial. The demonstration registers the host and enables the versioned AAP 2.7 repository that provides the ansible-dev-tools RPM.

prerequisites.label: Connectivity
prerequisites.detail: Outbound access to Red Hat registration and content services. Access to registry.redhat.io is also required when an execution-environment image is pulled. Configure any required proxy and trusted certificate chain before starting.

prerequisites.label: Starting state
prerequisites.detail: Begin with a fully updated RHEL 9 host where ansible-dev-tools, podman, and container-tools are not already installed. Use a fresh or reset lab system instead of removing unknown packages from a shared host.

prerequisiteCallouts.title: Don’t have a Red Hat subscription?
paragraphs: This demonstration requires access to both RHEL 9 and Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform. Eligible individuals can use the no-cost Red Hat Developer Subscription for RHEL. Apply separately for an AAP product trial, then use a Red Hat account with the required entitlements when registering the system so Subscription Manager can expose the RHEL and versioned AAP repositories.

The demonstration uses rhc connect for registration and rhc status for verification. Repository availability still depends on the account or organization having the required content access; contact the subscription administrator when registration succeeds but the AAP repository remains unavailable.

links.label: Apply for an AAP product trial

recap.title: What you learned
recap.introduction: The demonstration connects the purpose of ansible-dev-tools to evidence from a Red Hat-provided installation. Keep the package source, tool inventory, functional result, and remaining validation boundary together.

items.title: ADT coordinates a toolkit
items.detail: ansible-dev-tools brings independently released content-development utilities into one maintained installation request while the individual tools retain their own projects and responsibilities.

items.title: Distribution ownership matters
items.detail: This workflow uses Red Hat RPMs from an entitled AAP repository. An upstream Python installation follows a different package, update, and support path even when familiar commands are exposed.

items.title: Verification includes real work
items.detail: RPM queries and adt --version identify the installed toolchain, while ansible-creator and ansible-lint prove that two principal development functions work together.

items.title: The result has a boundary
items.detail: A generated and linted project does not prove execution-environment registry access, image builds, Molecule scenarios, signing workflows, controller integration, or remote automation readiness.

supportGuidance.title: Get help from the right owner
supportGuidance.introduction: Route a failure according to the component that owns it. Reproduce the problem, keep the installation path visible, and remove credentials, account identifiers, and private infrastructure details before sharing diagnostic output.

routes.title: RHEL connection, entitlement, repository, or RPM
routes.detail: Start with the organization team that owns Red Hat subscriptions and RHEL repositories. Use Red Hat support when the system has the required RHEL and AAP access and the problem falls within the documented product scope.

reference.label: Review the Red Hat RPM installation path

routes.title: Podman engine or container storage
routes.detail: Use the RHEL container-tools documentation and the platform team that owns the host, storage, networking, proxy, and registry configuration. A working Podman CLI alone does not prove image-pull or execution-environment readiness.

routes.title: Upstream development-tool defect
routes.detail: Identify the failing tool and exact version from adt --version, then review that project's documentation and existing issues. Report a reproducible upstream defect to the project that owns the command rather than treating ADT as one monolithic application.

reference.label: Review the upstream ADT tool list

routes.title: Custom playbook, role, collection, or test
routes.detail: Route content behavior to the team that owns the automation and its dependencies. Red Hat product support covers supported product behavior; it does not become the maintainer of custom automation content.

diagnostics.title: Collect evidence before requesting help
diagnostics.introduction: Run only the commands that apply to the failing layer. Review and redact their output before sharing it; never include passwords, tokens, account identifiers, or private infrastructure details.

items.command:
sudo rhc status
sudo subscription-manager repos --list-enabled
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
items.detail: Records the Red Hat service connection and enabled content sources without repeating registration or exposing credentials.

items.command:
sudo rpm -q ansible-dev-tools
sudo dnf info --installed ansible-dev-tools
items.detail: Captures the complete Red Hat package identity and the repository metadata for the installed toolchain.

items.command:
adt --version
type -a adt ansible-creator ansible-lint ansible-navigator
items.detail: Records the detected tool versions and every matching executable selected from the current PATH.
Separates a missing Podman executable from a container-engine, storage, networking, or rootless-runtime failure.
Re-runs the project validation with diagnostics visible and keeps Ansible cache state under the current user's home directory.

comparisons.title: Why install ansible-dev-tools instead of each tool separately?
comparisons.introduction: The development utilities are separate Python projects, and several depend on one another or share dependencies such as ansible-core and ansible-compat. Installing them one at a time leaves the developer to select versions, resolve conflicts, inventory the result, and retest the combined environment after every change. ansible-dev-tools makes that integration an explicit package boundary.

notes.title: One requested toolchain
notes.detail: A single ansible-dev-tools installation requests the maintained development utilities together. The Python or RPM package manager then resolves their declared requirements as one dependency graph instead of relying on a sequence of unrelated installation choices.

notes.title: Release order reflects shared dependencies
notes.detail: The upstream team releases lower-level projects before tools that depend on them, then releases ansible-dev-tools and validates the resulting Python package and container image. This coordination reduces the integration work that each developer would otherwise repeat.

notes.title: Coordinated does not mean permanently locked
notes.detail: The upstream package metadata mainly declares minimum versions, not an exact lock for every dependency. A fresh installation can therefore resolve newer compatible releases. Record the resolved versions, use an isolated environment, and retest the toolchain when its package set changes.

values: Select, install, and document every required utility separately. The list grows as a project adds scaffolding, linting, execution environments, signing, or test frameworks.
Request the curated toolchain through one package. The installation brings in the declared utilities and their supporting Python dependencies.
You own the combined version selection. Installing or upgrading one utility later can change shared dependencies or expose a requirement conflict with another tool.

The package manager evaluates the suite's declared requirements together and either finds a satisfiable set or reports the conflict. This reduces accidental combinations, but it cannot prove every project-specific workflow.
Track each project's releases and decide which combinations to test. Similar calendar-version numbers do not, by themselves, prove compatibility.

The upstream release process follows dependency order and validates the final ansible-dev-tools package and image. Red Hat separately selects and tests the package set delivered for an Ansible Automation Platform release.
Run each utility's version command and maintain your own inventory of the combined toolchain.
Use adt --version to see the versions of the content-development tools discovered in the current environment.
Exact pins, a constraints or lock file, and an isolated environment are your responsibility from the start.

ADT gives the environment a clear package boundary, but the upstream package is not a complete lock file. Capture exact resolved versions or use an image pinned by digest when identical rebuilds are required.
An individual tool can be upgraded independently, but every change must be checked against the rest of the shared environment.
Treat an ADT package or image update as one toolchain change. Review the resolved versions and run the project's lint, test, build, and execution checks before accepting it.
Best when a workflow needs only one or two utilities, or when a team deliberately maintains a custom version matrix. It has a smaller footprint but transfers integration ownership to that team.
Best when authors use several stages of the Ansible content-development workflow and want a discoverable, coordinated starting point. It installs more software than a single-purpose environment.

comparisons.takeawayLabel: Use the suite as a tested starting point
comparisons.takeaway: Install ansible-dev-tools when the work spans several development utilities and you want one maintained package boundary, one dependency-resolution transaction, and one version inventory. Install individual tools when the environment is intentionally narrow or governed by a custom compatibility matrix. In either case, isolate the environment, record exact resolved versions, and test the workflows your project actually uses.

comparisons.title: Upstream ansible-dev-tools vs Red Hat Ansible development tools
comparisons.introduction: Both paths use the Ansible development-tools ecosystem. The practical differences are how the software is delivered, which versions are selected and tested together, where it can run, and who supports the resulting installation.

notes.title: Curated tools are not the complete dependency graph
notes.detail: The ten tools above are the user-facing suite named by the upstream documentation. Package managers also install supporting Python libraries, and those transitive dependencies can change between releases.

notes.title: ansible-core is documented differently
notes.detail: Upstream ADT documentation includes ansible-core in the curated toolkit. Red Hat's development-workspace documentation lists ansible-core as a preinstalled runtime alongside the ADT package, then lists the remaining development tools under ADT. Do not assume that every delivery method has an identical direct dependency graph.

reference.label: Review the Red Hat workspace components

notes.title: Podman package or container-tools?
notes.detail: On RHEL 9, the podman package installs the container engine and its required dependencies. The container-tools meta-package installs Podman together with a broader toolkit that includes Buildah, Skopeo, CRIU, and Udica. They are not two editions of Podman. This demonstration installs podman because a working container engine is sufficient for ansible-navigator to use execution environments; install container-tools when the additional container utilities are also needed.

notes.title: Product support does not cover custom content
notes.detail: Red Hat support applies to shipped products and supported usage within the published scope. The AAP support policy lists custom content and custom collection development or debugging outside standard product support.

reference.label: Review the AAP scope of support

notes.title: Check the Python requirement for the selected release
notes.detail: The current PyPI package metadata requires Python 3.11 or later, while the general upstream installation page still states Python 3.10 or later. Package documentation can lag a release, so check the Requires-Python metadata for the exact ansible-dev-tools version before choosing an interpreter.

reference.label: Review the current PyPI package metadata

comparisons.summaryLabel: Compare upstream and Red Hat delivery

values: A Python distribution published on PyPI. The upstream project also publishes the community-ansible-dev-tools container image through GitHub Container Registry.
An RPM delivered through versioned Ansible Automation Platform repositories, plus Red Hat development-container and development-workspace options.
Install ansible-dev-tools from PyPI into an isolated Python environment. The current package metadata requires Python 3.11 or later.
Install the ansible-dev-tools RPM with DNF on supported RHEL, or use the downstream development container selected by the Ansible VS Code extension.
PyPI packages, upstream source, and the community container are publicly available without an Ansible Automation Platform subscription.
RPM repositories and authenticated images require the appropriate Red Hat access. Product support requires an active Ansible Automation Platform subscription.
Upstream releases follow the community project's cadence. Python resolves the declared requirements and compatible transitive dependencies at installation time.
Red Hat selects, builds, tests, and updates a compatible package set for an Ansible Automation Platform release. Its versions do not have to match the newest PyPI releases.
The Python distribution is described as operating-system independent, subject to Python and individual tool requirements. The community container is based on Fedora Minimal.
The local RPM path targets supported RHEL. The downstream VS Code development container uses a supported Red Hat base image and can be launched from supported Linux, macOS, or Windows hosts.
pip or another Python installer resolves packages from Python indexes. Use a virtual environment, pipx, or another isolated workflow to avoid mixing them with system Python packages.
DNF installs Red Hat-built RPM dependencies from enabled repositories. The downstream container and development workspace arrive with a preconfigured, tested tool environment.
Choose when to upgrade the Python package or pull a new community image. Read upstream release notes and retest projects when the toolchain changes.
Consume updates through Red Hat RPM or image channels appropriate to the selected AAP release, following the applicable Red Hat lifecycle and update guidance.
Community support is provided through upstream documentation, forums, Matrix, and project issue trackers. There is no Red Hat product-support entitlement for this installation path.

Red Hat supports the productized packages and supported development environments within the scope and lifecycle of the customer's Ansible Automation Platform subscription. This does not extend product support to custom automation content.
Useful for contributors, evaluation, cross-platform development, and teams that prefer the current upstream toolchain and manage their own compatibility testing.
Useful when an organization needs Red Hat-tested package combinations, controlled repositories or images, documented platform requirements, and vendor support.

comparisons.takeawayLabel: Choose by delivery and support requirements
comparisons.takeaway: Choose the upstream distribution when you want the upstream release cadence and will own environment compatibility. Choose the Red Hat distribution when you have an Ansible Automation Platform subscription and need Red Hat-tested artifacts, lifecycle guidance, and product support. The commands may look familiar in either environment, but package provenance and support coverage are not interchangeable.

comparisons.title: Operate the selected development toolchain
comparisons.introduction: The installation method establishes an ownership and change model. Record the accepted tool versions, use one package-management path, test project workflows after updates, and keep the last accepted baseline available until the replacement passes validation.

values: The Python-environment owner controls the interpreter, isolated environment, package index, resolved dependencies, and upgrade schedule.
The image owner controls the selected tag or digest, registry access, image scanning, local storage, and replacement schedule.
The RHEL platform owner controls entitlements, enabled AAP repositories, DNF transactions, advisories, and the supported host baseline.
Record the Python version, ansible-dev-tools package metadata, dependency health, and adt --version output inside the isolated environment.
Record the image registry, repository, immutable digest, creation metadata, and adt --version output from the running container.
Record rpm -q ansible-dev-tools, dnf info --installed ansible-dev-tools, adt --version, and the Podman engine result.
Build and test a replacement isolated environment from reviewed requirements. Do not upgrade a shared system Python environment in place.
Pull a reviewed replacement image, verify its digest, scan it under organizational policy, and test it before changing the approved reference.
Review available Red Hat updates and advisories, apply the approved DNF transaction, then repeat package, engine, create, lint, and project-specific tests.
Pin direct and transitive packages when an equivalent rebuild is required, and record the Python version separately.
Use an immutable image digest when identical image selection matters; a moving tag does not preserve the accepted artifact.
Record name, epoch, version, release, architecture, repository, and advisory. Reproduction depends on the required RPMs remaining in an approved repository or content-management system.
Retain the last accepted environment until its replacement passes. Remove only the isolated environment after confirming that no workflow uses it.
Keep the prior approved digest until the replacement passes. Removing a container or image does not remove bind-mounted projects or external registry content.
Inspect DNF history before recovery. Removing ansible-dev-tools or Podman does not automatically remove every dependency, cache, image, configuration file, or generated project.

comparisons.takeawayLabel: Keep one owner and one change channel
comparisons.takeaway: Do not mix pip-installed packages into the Red Hat RPM-owned environment or mutate an accepted container in place. Capture the exact accepted state, test changes in a replacement environment when practical, and preserve the former baseline until validation succeeds.

demos.title: Install Red Hat ansible-dev-tools on RHEL 9
demos.objective: Register RHEL, enable the matching Ansible Automation Platform repository, install the Red Hat ansible-dev-tools RPM, inventory its toolchain, and validate a generated project.
demos.coverAlt: Red Hat AAP repository delivering ansible-dev-tools to a RHEL 9 workstation for project creation and linting
outcomes: Connect RHEL to Red Hat services and enable the architecture-matched AAP 2.7 repository
Install Podman and the Red Hat ansible-dev-tools RPM
Verify the principal tool packages and their active versions
Create an Ansible project and validate it with ansible-lint
demos.validationBoundary: This proves that the Red Hat ansible-dev-tools RPM and its principal tool packages are installed, their commands are discoverable, and a generated playbook project passes ansible-lint. It does not validate registry authentication, execution-environment builds or pulls, Molecule scenarios, signing workflows, controller integration, or remote automation readiness.
nextActions: Save the RPM identities, adt --version output, Podman version, and project validation result with the development-environment notes.
Keep DNF and the enabled AAP repository as the owners of this Red Hat-provided toolchain.
Repeat the package inventory, project generation, and lint validation after approved toolchain updates.
Configure approved registry access and validate execution-environment workflows before relying on containerized automation.

relatedHod.title: Looking for the upstream installation path?
relatedHod.detail: HOD 001 demonstrates Python virtual-environment and pipx isolation concepts, not exact ansible-dev-tools installation commands. Upstream ADT documentation uses pip in an isolated Python environment. If pipx is selected instead, remember that dependency applications such as ansible-lint and ansible-navigator are not exposed by default; review pipx dependency-app options and verify every required command.

steps.label: System Baseline
steps.title: Inspect the RHEL 9 starting environment
steps.alt: Terminal identifying RHEL 9, the system architecture, hostname, and clean development-tool and container package state
steps.explanation: Begin with a clear picture of the control node before changing it. This establishes the platform and architecture used in the demonstration and whether ansible-dev-tools or a container package is already present.

commands.explanation: Reads the RHEL release file to identify the installed operating-system name and major release.
Reports the processor architecture, which determines which architecture-specific repositories and packages apply to the host.
Displays the static hostname so learners can identify the control node used in the demonstration.
Queries the RPM database and confirms whether ansible-dev-tools is already installed.
Checks both RHEL container-package paths so an existing Podman installation cannot silently change the later DNF transaction.

steps.expected: The host reports RHEL 9, its architecture and hostname, followed by package-not-installed results for ansible-dev-tools, podman, and container-tools.
steps.note: This recording uses aarch64. Select the x86_64 repository later when uname -m reports x86_64.
steps.troubleshooting: Stop if this is not RHEL 9 or if any checked package is already installed. Reset the lab or use a separate clean system instead of removing unknown software from a shared host.

recovery.detail: Use a supported RHEL 9 lab host for this recorded RPM workflow. Do not adapt the repository command until the target platform and product documentation have been reviewed.
Treat the host as an existing installation and use the package, inventory, and functional verification steps. Reset a disposable lab before following the installation transaction.

recovery.symptom: podman or container-tools is already installed
recovery.detail: Record the existing package identity and let the platform owner decide whether the later Podman step should become an update or verification. Do not remove it automatically on a shared system.

steps.label: Register RHEL
steps.title: Register RHEL with Red Hat services
steps.alt: RHEL terminal confirming successful connections to Red Hat services
steps.explanation: A registered RHEL system can retrieve protected content from Red Hat repositories. This demonstration uses an interactive Red Hat account login and keeps all credential input outside the published replay.

commands.explanation: Runs the Red Hat connector with administrative privileges. It registers the system with Subscription Management and connects it to Red Hat Lightspeed.

steps.expected: rhc reports successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Lightspeed and activates remote host configuration. The recorded client uses the former Red Hat Insights name in its output.
steps.note: Credential input is excluded from the replay. The neutral placeholders show where learners interact without exposing an account name or password.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the message returned by rhc connect to distinguish an interactive-login problem from a registration or service-connection failure.

recovery.detail: Run rhc connect from an interactive terminal. A background process or non-interactive shell cannot accept the Red Hat account prompts.
Confirm network access, DNS, proxy configuration, system time, and an active RHEL entitlement, then retry this registration step.

steps.label: Verify Connection
steps.title: Verify the Red Hat connection
steps.alt: RHEL terminal showing active Subscription Management and Red Hat hosted inventory connections
steps.explanation: Registration should be confirmed independently before relying on protected repositories. The connection status separates a successful login from a usable registered system.

commands.explanation: Reports the system's current connections to Subscription Management, Red Hat Lightspeed, and remote host configuration services.

steps.expected: The recorded system is connected to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Lightspeed. The recorded client uses the former Red Hat Insights name, and remote host configuration may be inactive.
steps.note: Subscription Management is required for DNF repository access. Red Hat Lightspeed and remote host configuration are separate services; their state does not determine whether DNF can use subscribed repositories.
steps.troubleshooting: Read each rhc status line separately. Return to registration when Subscription Management is disconnected; do not treat an inactive Lightspeed or remote host configuration connection as a DNF repository failure.

recovery.detail: Return to the interactive registration step, confirm the entitled RHEL account and network path, then repeat the connection check.
recovery.command:
sudo rhc connect
sudo rhc status

recovery.symptom: Only Lightspeed or remote host configuration is inactive
recovery.detail: Continue with the DNF workflow when Subscription Management is connected. Investigate the other service only when the organization uses that capability.

steps.label: Enable Repository
steps.title: Enable the AAP 2.7 repository
steps.alt: Terminal enabling the AArch64 Ansible Automation Platform 2.7 repository
steps.explanation: Enable the versioned AAP repository that supplies Red Hat ansible-dev-tools packages. The repository ID must match the host architecture.

commands.explanation: Enables the AAP 2.7 RPM repository for an AArch64 RHEL 9 host without listing unrelated repositories.

steps.expected: Subscription Manager reports that the AAP 2.7 AArch64 repository is enabled.
steps.note: On x86_64, use ansible-automation-platform-2.7-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms instead. Do not copy the recorded architecture blindly.
steps.troubleshooting: A missing repository normally indicates a mismatched architecture, absent AAP entitlement, or stale subscription data.

recovery.detail: Confirm uname -m, refresh subscription data, and use the corresponding entitled repository ID.

steps.label: Install Podman
steps.title: Install Podman as the container engine
steps.alt: DNF transaction installing Podman on RHEL 9
steps.explanation: Install Podman before the development toolkit so ansible-navigator and ansible-builder have a container engine for execution-environment workflows.

commands.explanation: Installs the Podman engine and required dependencies from enabled RHEL repositories.

steps.expected: DNF completes the Podman installation successfully.
steps.note: The podman package is sufficient here. The broader container-tools meta-package also installs Buildah, Skopeo, CRIU, and Udica.
steps.troubleshooting: Resolve repository, metadata, download, dependency, or signature errors reported by DNF; do not bypass package-signature checks.

recovery.symptom: DNF cannot find or download Podman
recovery.detail: Confirm the enabled RHEL repositories and available storage, then retry only after the repository or connectivity problem is resolved.
Do not remove it merely to match the video. Record the installed identity, confirm that it is approved, and continue to the functional engine check.

steps.label: Inspect Package
steps.title: Inspect the Red Hat package metadata
steps.alt: DNF information for the available Red Hat ansible-dev-tools package
steps.explanation: Review the package source, version, architecture, size, and description before approving a system change.

commands.explanation: Displays metadata for the ansible-dev-tools RPM available from the enabled AAP repository.

steps.expected: DNF finds the noarch ansible-dev-tools package in the enabled AAP 2.7 repository that matches the host architecture.
steps.troubleshooting: If no package is found, revisit the repository step and confirm entitlement, architecture, and current DNF metadata.

recovery.detail: Refresh DNF metadata after confirming the correct AAP repository is enabled, then repeat the query.
recovery.command:
sudo dnf clean metadata
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf info ansible-dev-tools

steps.label: Install Toolchain
steps.title: Install Red Hat ansible-dev-tools
steps.alt: DNF completing the Red Hat ansible-dev-tools installation
steps.explanation: Let DNF resolve the coordinated Red Hat package set and review the transaction before approving the installation.

commands.explanation: Installs the ansible-dev-tools RPM and its required Red Hat-built dependencies from enabled repositories.

steps.expected: The transaction finishes with Complete! and includes ansible-dev-tools among the installed packages.
steps.note: This recording installed 89 packages. Treat that count and all versions as observed evidence, not a permanent product guarantee.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the DNF error to identify metadata, dependency, download, storage, or signature problems before retrying the transaction.

recovery.symptom: The package transaction cannot resolve dependencies
recovery.detail: Preserve the DNF error, confirm that enabled repositories belong to the approved RHEL and AAP release, and avoid mixing Python packages into the RPM-owned environment.
recovery.command:
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf info ansible-dev-tools

recovery.symptom: A download or metadata operation fails
recovery.detail: Check network, proxy, certificate, repository, and storage conditions. Refresh metadata only after the underlying access problem has been corrected.
recovery.command:
df -h
sudo dnf clean metadata
sudo dnf makecache

steps.label: Verify Packages
steps.title: Verify the installed RPM packages
steps.alt: RPM queries confirming the installed Ansible development tool packages
steps.explanation: Verify the principal user-facing components through the RPM database. This proves package ownership and records the Red Hat build identities installed on the host.

commands.explanation: Prints the installed ansible-dev-tools RPM name, version, release, and architecture.
Queries the main Ansible command-line and content-development RPMs installed with the toolkit.
Queries the Python-versioned RPMs that provide pytest-ansible and tox-ansible in this package set.
Records the installed ansible-dev-tools and Podman versions, architectures, source RPMs, and originating repositories for the accepted workstation baseline.

steps.expected: Every RPM query returns an installed package identity, and DNF identifies the AAP repository for ansible-dev-tools plus the RHEL AppStream repository for Podman.
steps.note: Python-versioned RPM names and exact repository package builds can change in a later supported package set. Record the identities supplied by the current approved repositories rather than assuming these values indefinitely.
steps.troubleshooting: A missing package should be checked against the completed DNF transaction and the dependencies of the currently available ansible-dev-tools build.

recovery.detail: Inspect the most recent DNF transaction and installed-package metadata before attempting another installation.
recovery.command:

recovery.detail: Compare the missing RPM with the currently installed ansible-dev-tools dependency set. Package names and Python-versioned providers can change between supported builds.

steps.label: Inventory Toolchain
steps.title: Inventory the toolchain and verify Podman
steps.alt: ADT and Podman commands reporting tool versions and a working rootless container engine
steps.explanation: Record the executable versions visible to the current shell, then verify that Podman can initialize its engine and inspect the current rootless runtime. This complements RPM package verification with functional runtime evidence.

commands.explanation: Reports the installed ansible-dev-tools version and inventories the tool versions detected in the active environment.
Confirms that the Podman executable starts and prints its active version.
Initializes the Podman engine and reports the host platform plus whether the current user is operating rootlessly, without printing the full engine inventory.

steps.expected: adt prints a populated development-tool inventory, Podman reports its version, and the engine check identifies the host platform with Rootless: true.
steps.note: adt --version describes the current environment; it does not lock those versions or replace dependency and lifecycle controls. Podman engine initialization does not prove registry authentication, image pulls, or execution-environment compatibility.
steps.troubleshooting: If a command is missing, compare the RPM queries in the prior step with the executable path resolved by the current shell. If podman info fails, preserve its storage, namespace, or runtime error for the host owner.

recovery.symptom: An installed executable is not found
recovery.detail: Clear cached command paths and inspect every matching executable before changing packages.

recovery.symptom: Podman reports an engine or storage error
recovery.detail: Keep the complete podman info error and route it to the RHEL container-platform owner. Do not switch to sudo merely to hide a rootless-runtime problem.

steps.label: Create Project
steps.title: Create an Ansible playbook project
steps.alt: ansible-creator generating a playbook project under the user home directory
steps.explanation: Move beyond version checks by using ansible-creator to scaffold a real project. This validates that an installed development tool can perform its primary function.

commands.explanation: Creates a reusable parent directory for Ansible development projects without failing if it already exists.
Changes into the parent directory so the generated project is created in a predictable location.
Uses ansible-creator to scaffold adt-demo with the branded example namespace rajat.demo; substitute your own valid namespace when adapting the project.

steps.expected: ansible-creator reports a successful initialization and creates ~/ansible-projects/adt-demo.
steps.note: The rajat.demo value is an Ansible content namespace used for this recorded example, not a home-directory path or a requirement to use the rajat operating-system account. Replace it with the namespace approved for your own content.
steps.troubleshooting: If creation fails, preserve the error and check whether the destination already contains a partial project before retrying.

recovery.detail: Inspect the existing directory and choose a different disposable project name rather than overwriting unknown work.

steps.label: Lint Project
steps.title: Validate the generated project with ansible-lint
steps.alt: ansible-lint completing successfully for the generated site playbook
steps.explanation: Finish with a functional lint check against the generated playbook. A clean result proves that the project and linting tool can work together.

commands.explanation: Changes into the generated project directory so its files and configuration are the active linting context.

commands.command: ANSIBLE_HOME="$HOME/.ansible" ansible-lint site.yml && echo "Verified: ansible-lint passed"
commands.explanation: Checks site.yml with Ansible cache state under the current user's home directory and prints an explicit confirmation only when ansible-lint exits successfully.

steps.expected: ansible-lint reports zero failures and zero warnings, followed by Verified: ansible-lint passed.
steps.note: The confirmation is joined with &&, so it appears only after a successful lint result. Standard error remains visible for troubleshooting.
steps.troubleshooting: Treat any rule violation as project feedback and keep the diagnostic output visible. If the executable fails to start, return to the package and tool-inventory checks.

recovery.detail: Read the rule identifier and file location, correct the generated or modified content, then repeat the same validation. Do not suppress the finding to obtain a passing result.

recovery.symptom: ansible-lint fails before evaluating the file
recovery.detail: Re-run with verbose diagnostics while retaining the portable user-owned Ansible cache path, then use the error to distinguish project, executable, dependency, and environment failures.

cleanup.explanation: Cleanup is optional on a disposable lab VM. Removing the named packages is not a complete rollback: dependencies, caches, container images, configuration, and files under ~/ansible-projects can remain. If the host remains registered but should no longer consume AAP development-tool content, disable the architecture-matched repository used by the installation. Disconnect only when the host should no longer consume subscribed content.
cleanup.command:
sudo dnf remove ansible-dev-tools podman
# Optional: disable the repository used by this AArch64 recording
sudo subscription-manager repos --disable="ansible-automation-platform-2.7-for-rhel-9-aarch64-rpms"
# Optional: disconnect this disposable lab VM
sudo rhc disconnect
